title: How do you prepare stories for the consulting fit interview?
description: Behavioural questions often count as much as the case. Build 6-8 stories once, and use each for several questions.
hook: The fit interview is often treated as the easy part, and that is why people stumble on it. Interviewers want real stories about real moments in your life, told clearly and honestly. This guide shows you how to build a handful of stories once and use them for almost any question.
body:
In this guide

  • What firms are looking for
  • STAR-L: the story shape
  • Build a story bank
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

What firms are looking for

Most fit questions test the same handful of qualities: leadership (do people follow you when it's hard?), impact (did things change because of you?), initiative (do you start things?), persuasion (can you bring people round?) and how you handle failure. McKinsey's version, the Personal Experience Interview (PEI), goes deep on one story at a time, so expect follow-up questions.

STAR-L: the story shape

  • Situation: the context, in one or two lines.
  • Task: what you were responsible for.
  • Action: what you did, step by step. This is the heart of the story; say "I", not "we".
  • Result: what changed, with a number if possible.
  • Learning: what you'd do differently.

Aim for 90-120 seconds per story, told, never read.

Build a story bank

Write 6-8 stories and map each to the questions it can answer. One strong story often covers leadership, conflict and impact. Rehearse out loud weekly. Your "Tell me about yourself" (60-90 seconds) and "Why this firm?" (with specifics: people you spoke to, practice areas) need preparing too.

See it in action: The action section, done well

"I rebuilt the pricing model over a weekend, then split the remaining work by each person's strengths rather than seniority. I went to the manager with a proposal to drop two low-value analyses, and set up a 15-minute daily check-in so problems surfaced early."

Specific, first person, and every sentence is something you did.

What to remember

  • 6-8 stories cover most questions.
  • The action section is the heart: specific, first person.
  • Quantify the result; finish with what you learned.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. Which part of a STAR-L story deserves the most time?

  • Situation
  • Action
  • Learning
Show the answer

Action. The interviewer is assessing what you did. Keep context short.

Try it now

Write the Action part of a story about persuading someone you had no authority over. Three sentences, each starting with "I".

Give yourself 2 minutes, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

"I asked the regional head for 20 minutes to understand what worried her about the change. I rebuilt the proposal around her two concerns and ran a two-week pilot in one team so she could see the results. I shared the numbers with her first, before anyone else, so the decision to roll it out was hers."
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 11 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
